Mardi 14 mai. Une foule où dominent les: Tuesday, May 14. A crowd dominated by shades of blue and white fills Place du Canada in downtown Montréal. A few streets away, festive music can be heard coming from the stage and speakers at the celebration of the 76<sup>th</sup> anniversary of Israel's independence.
Alors que certains célèbrent, d’autres f: While some celebrate, others mourn. On the other side of René-Lévesque Boulevard, at Dorchester Square, demonstrators have organized a counter-demonstration. While Israel's independence means freedom for many, and the liberation of a people who fully hold the right to exist, it reminds others of the sorrowful Nakba, Arabic for “catastrophe”: the exodus during which hundreds of thousands of Palestinians had to leave their native land and go into exile.
Au centre de ces deux réalités, Montréal: Caught between these two realities, Montréal reacts. Police officers are deployed on site and set up a security perimeter on each side of the boulevard, ensuring that the peace is kept between the two gatherings. But who are these people who turn out, despite the rain and bad weather, to celebrate Israel or to commemorate the Nakba? La Converse went there to try to understand what moves these Montrealers to mobilize, some for Israelis, others for Palestinians.
Sur la Place du Canada, des Montréalais: At Place du Canada, Montrealers gather to celebrate Israel's anniversary. Photo: Melissa Haouari
<strong>« Nous ne sommes pas seulement p: “We are not just pro-Israel, we are Israel!”
« Aujourd’hui, nous célébrons la victoir: “Today, we celebrate Israel's victory over the British Empire, when we liberated our ancestral lands,” Montréal activist Ysabella Hazan shouts to a fired-up crowd. “We are not just pro-Israel, we are Israel!” she adds in a firm voice.
Sur la scène érigée au milieu, des centa: In front of the stage set up in the middle, hundreds of people applaud and sing. Despite the rain, everyone has gathered to hear speeches on Israeli solidarity by Ysabella Hazan and Jeremy Levi, the mayor of Hampstead.
Dans un Montréal tendu, surtout depuis q: In a tense Montréal, especially over the past few weeks, since pro-Palestinian encampments were set up on the grounds of some of the city's universities, many people there say how important it is to them to attend the celebration. “For six months, Jews have been afraid to go out,” Josh, a young man taking part in the celebrations, tells us. “Students are afraid to go to school. We're afraid to go downtown, to go to class, to do activities… So today, we're showing that we're here and that we're proud to be Jewish,” he adds.
Julien, un autre étudiant de confession: Julien, another Jewish student, came to celebrate his heritage. He believes the atmosphere at his university is tense. “I've heard a lot of stories and I see a lot of things. I see labels everywhere. It's very intimidating,” he confides, worried.
Malgré tout, il reste optimiste : « Il f: Still, he remains optimistic: “We have to stay proud, we have to stay brave. If we truly believe in Israel, we can't give up and hide.”

Au même moment, de l’autre côté du boule: At the same time, on the other side of René-Lévesque Boulevard, the atmosphere seems gloomier. This is not only due to the greater number of trees at Dorchester Square overlooking the space, but also to the sadder, more severe faces of the people.
La foule est plus petite, mais le messag: The crowd is smaller, but the message is heavy. The slogans “Free Palestine” and “Yes to Judaism, no to Zionism” ring out, chanted through megaphones by activists.
En première ligne, le rabbin Dovid Feldm: On the front line, Rabbi Dovid Feldman proudly raises his sign, which shows an Israeli flag crossed out with a bright red line. He is accompanied by three of his colleagues, all members of the organization Jews United Against Zionism.
« Nous sommes-là par tristesse » – tels: “We are here out of sadness”: those are the first words Rabbi Feldman, his organization's spokesperson, says to us. He tells us he is originally from New York and came to Montréal specially to commemorate the Nakba and denounce the situation in Gaza.
Outré par la célébration israélienne, qu: Outraged by the Israeli celebration taking place barely a few dozen metres from him, the New Yorker says he is “troubled and disturbed by the event across the way.” He explains: “There is nothing to celebrate. It's sad. When we are witnessing a genocide that has been going on for seven months in Gaza, where tens of thousands of innocent men, women and children are being murdered en masse, there is nothing to celebrate,” he says in one breath.
Sur la même lancée, il ajoute qu’« il ne: Continuing in the same vein, he adds that “this is not only a violation of international law, but also a violation of Judaism.” The religious leader also believes that “condemning these crimes is not antisemitic, as some might sometimes think. It's a just cause, no matter who the perpetrators are!”
Le lendemain, les rues du centre-ville s: The next day, downtown streets are packed with Nakba demonstrators. Photo: Édouard Desroches
Mercredi 15 mai. Au lendemain des célébr: Wednesday, May 15. The day after the celebrations marking Israel's independence, hundreds of demonstrators gather again at Dorchester Square, this time to commemorate the Nakba, the territorial dispossession of non-Jewish Palestinians in 1948.
Alors que la foule se rassemble avant d’: As the crowd assembles before setting off along a route through the city's streets, a spokesperson for the march's organizers exclaims: “The Nakba will be renamed ‘Palestinian Resistance Day’!”
Parmi les manifestants, il y a Yara, une: Among the demonstrators is Yara, a student of Palestinian origin. Today, she feels “overwhelmed.” Surrounded by noise and moving along with the march, she tells us that her grandparents were expelled from Palestine in 1948. “My mother is originally from Gaza. I had family there, in fact. Today, some of them, like my aunt and my cousins, have taken refuge in Egypt,” she says.
Plus jeune, elle était entourée d’amis q: When she was younger, she was surrounded by friends who spent their summer holidays in their countries of origin. “Everyone was looking forward to going back to France or Lebanon, for example, to spend time with family. I was always the only one who had nowhere to go. It was very frustrating,” she recalls.
Accompagnée de son amie, Yara raconte le: Accompanied by her friend, Yara describes the damage caused by the conflicts between the Arab countries and Israel. Today, she sees the liberation movement as an ongoing process. “It's a battle that continues. And this battle must go on until Palestine is free,” she says.

Ihmayed Ali connaît bien la résistance p: Ihmayed Ali knows Palestinian resistance well. He is taking part in the demonstration with his sister and some of his relatives.
« Je suis ici, car je suis un témoin pal: “I am here because I am a Palestinian witness to the catastrophe,” he says. “My family was expelled from Palestine in 1948. They fled north, then to Lebanon, before living in a refugee camp, where I was born.”
Lorsque Ihmayedl était enfant, lui et sa: When Ihmayed was a child, he and his family did not have access to many resources as refugees. “I remember we all lived in one room, without electricity. We had no kitchen and no bathroom, nothing. There was no support, no help, except from UNRWA (the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East), which provided us with basic necessities, like food and medicine,” he remembers.
Le père de famille a choisi d’immigrer a: The father chose to immigrate to Canada to give his children a better education. He says his children have more opportunities here, but he still hopes to find his way back to his native land one day. “We are here today to tell everyone that we are refugees and that we have the right to return to our country,” he says. He is referring to United Nations Resolution 194, which allows all refugees to return to live in their country of origin.
Ihmayed se dit toutefois extrêmement rec: Ihmayed says, however, that he is extremely grateful for the solidarity with Palestinians he has observed over the years in Quebec. “I love Quebec, because Quebecers support us much more than you'd imagine. Every day, they are out in the streets demonstrating for Palestinian rights. I hope to return to Palestine one day and be able to welcome all these people into my home the same way I was welcomed here,” he concludes with a smile.

Alors que les manifestants descendent le: As the demonstrators head down René-Lévesque Boulevard, members of Lawyers for Palestine, a collective of lawyers supporting the Palestinian cause, hold a banner showing the colours of the Palestinian flag. Dressed in their black robes, they take up the crowd's chants wholeheartedly.
L’un d’entre eux est clair : « La loi in: One of them is clear: “International law says it in black and white: Israel is guilty of an illegal occupation of Palestinian land,” he says. The lawyer, who does not give his first name during this exchange, believes the “struggle for liberation must continue.”
« Si on suit le principe que, si quelque: “If we follow the principle that if some are oppressed, all are oppressed, then we will never achieve peace in a world where imperialism and colonialism exist,” he explains.
Sur la rue Crescent, où la marche se dir: On Crescent Street, where the march is heading, restaurant and shop terraces are filled with curious onlookers watching the approaching crowd. The demonstration's leaders, armed with megaphones, shout loudly to everyone: “The taxes you pay on your meal and your pints are funding a genocide!”
